### Adjusted vs Bivariate Associations

_In plain terms:_ each predictor gets two numbers — a _bivariate_ association (its raw link to the outcome on its own) and an _adjusted_ association (the same link after holding the other predictors constant). Comparing them shows how much of a raw relationship survives once overlapping predictors are accounted for. These are adjusted associations, not causal effects.

```{python}
# | echo: false
predictor_associations = _csv("predictor_associations.csv")
predictor_associations if predictor_associations is not None else "No predictor associations."
```

_How to read the table:_ one row per predictor. The bivariate columns are the predictor's standalone link to the outcome; the adjusted columns are the same link with the other predictors held fixed. Each estimate carries an 89% credible interval (the range the value plausibly falls in); an interval that stays on one side of zero points to a consistent direction.

```{python}
# | echo: false
# | output: asis
print(_img("predictor_associations.png", "Adjusted vs bivariate associations"))
print(f"\n_How to read the plot:_ one row per baseline predictor. Each row shows two estimates of its standardised association with the modelled {outcome_label} gain (per-SD, on the logit scale): the blue circle is the *adjusted* coefficient with the other predictors held constant, the grey square the *bivariate* coefficient on its own; the bars are 89% credible intervals. The dotted line at 0 is no association — markers to its right associate with more gain, to the left with less, and a bar crossing it means the sign is uncertain. When the blue circle sits closer to 0 than the grey square, adjustment has absorbed part of that raw link. Read every marker as an adjusted association, not a causal effect.")
```

### Natural-Scale Differences

_In plain terms:_ this puts the associations back on the outcome's item scale — how many items the outcome differs by for a one-SD difference in each predictor — so the size is readable without thinking in standardised units.

```{python}
# | echo: false
# | output: asis
if _adjusted_plan.get("transition_waves"):
    print("_Where the contrast is taken:_ each row is averaged over the fitted transition rows at their observed covariates, with the child random intercept at zero — a row-averaged, median-child contrast. The prior pushforward in the priors section uses the same functional.")
else:
    _ref_group = " and the reading-group dummies at zero (the reference group)" if config.get("study_id") == "rlm" else ""
    print(f"_Where the contrast is taken:_ each row is evaluated at one operating point — a child at the sample-mean own baseline with every other standardised predictor at zero{_ref_group} — for two such children who differ by one SD on one predictor. On a logit-scale model the same coefficient gives a somewhat different item difference elsewhere on the scale; the prior pushforward in the priors section uses this same at-the-mean functional.")
```

_How to read the table:_ each row translates a predictor's association into a difference in outcome items, with its 89% credible interval. Read it as "how much the outcome differs by", an adjusted association on a plain scale — not a caused gain. Missing-data indicators are nuisance subgroup offsets and are not listed here.

### Sensitivity Checks

_In plain terms:_ these checks ask whether the conclusions hold up when the prior on the predictor slopes is loosened, and when the own-baseline coupling prior — the one prior centred away from zero, at a 1:1 coupling — is widened. The RLI model additionally checks socioeconomic-status (SES) adjustment; the Byrne cohort models do not have that SES sensitivity. Estimates that barely move are less dependent on the prior choice; ones that swing are more prior-sensitive.

```{python}
# | echo: false
prior_sensitivity = _csv("prior_sensitivity.csv")
prior_sensitivity if prior_sensitivity is not None else "No prior-sensitivity table."
```

_How to read the table:_ each row re-fits under a different prior setting (the assumption fed in before seeing the data): `predictor_slope_sigma` is the SD of the slope prior, `gamma_own_sigma` the SD of the own-baseline coupling prior (the first block of rows is the fitted model itself). Compare the estimates across rows — small shifts mean the data, not the prior, is doing the work.


### Influence

_In plain terms:_ this flags whether any single child is pulling the results — the children whose removal would move the leave-one-out fit the most, measured by the PSIS-LOO Pareto-k value.

```{python}
# | echo: false
# | output: asis
influence = _csv("influence.csv")
_pareto = _csv("pareto_k.csv")
_flag_threshold = None
_n_flagged = None
if _pareto is not None and {"pareto_k", "good_k_threshold"}.issubset(_pareto.columns):
    _k = pd.to_numeric(_pareto["pareto_k"], errors="coerce")
    _flag_threshold = float(pd.to_numeric(_pareto["good_k_threshold"], errors="coerce").iloc[0])
    _n_flagged = int((_k > _flag_threshold).sum())
if _adjusted_plan.get("transition_waves"):
    print("_What the unit is here:_ the LOO is **child-level** — each child's transition rows are left out together and the child's random intercept is integrated away (new-child prediction). Importance sampling handles that target poorly under a per-child intercept, so a substantial share of flagged children is the expected failure mode of the LOO score, not evidence against the sampler or the reported associations; the score should not be used for model comparison while children are flagged.")
else:
    print("_What the unit is here:_ one row per child, so each point is one child left out.")
if _flag_threshold is not None and _n_flagged is not None:
    print(f"\n{_n_flagged} of {len(_pareto)} leave-one-out points exceed the Pareto-k reliability threshold {_flag_threshold:.2f}.")
if influence is not None:
    display(influence.head(10))
    print("\n_How to read the table:_ rows are the most influential children (top ten), ranked by Pareto-k — how much dropping each one would shift the leave-one-out fit. Values above the threshold warrant a look; if even the top rows are small, no one child is driving the conclusions.")
else:
    print("\n_No per-child influence table was written for this fit._")
```
